Q: What does the use of the "+" and "*" operators on lists mean? A:

Note: I won't talk about the function itself, how to optimize it, how to fix it, etc. Answers already explains what is does, without addressing what it is and what it means.

I'll try to answer the exact question OP had.

This is a code I saw for avaluating fibonacci number using memoization, what does [0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) mean? Can you please explain me what does this type of writing represent?

[0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) is specifically a way to pre-allocate the list your function needs to create, instead of increasing its size when adding new elements everytime it computes a new one as this function would:

def fib_mem(n, result = None):
    if result is None:
        result = [0, 1]
    if len(result) < n+2:
        fib_mem(n-1, result)
        result.append(result[-1] + result[-2])
    return result[n]

Here, you already know the final size the list will have before you even start: n+2. So, instead of reallocating the list memory from a size 2 to n+2, you allocate it filled with placeholder values.

That's all. You don't need it to memoïze the fib computation, as the function I just showed do use memoïzation and compute fib(1000) almost instantly, but it helps reducing the memory reallocation of the list.

[0,1]+[-1]*(n-1) could have been [0,1]+[None]*(n-1), [0,1]+["yolo"]*(n-1) or anything, as its sole purpose is to make the list the desired size from the start. Its content doesn't matter (except the first two values of course) when it is initialized.

Q: Merging two sorted skip lists into a third one can be done in O(n)? A:

This "answer" (like others here) failed to address the intended topic, merging two skip lists.
I had never heard of skip lists. I thought a "skip list" might be a list of things to "skip". A skip list is a data structure that holds ordered data and allows rapid searching and inserting. It is not a tree.

This "answer" addresses merging two sorted lists, a very old concept. (Coincidentally, I stumbled upon the idea of looking ahead to speed up, which is one of the things that skip lists facilitate.)
(The sizes of the sorted input lists are m and n.)
Worst-case, you need m + n - 1 comparisons to merge the lists. O(m+n).
Best-case, IF the ranges don't overlap at all, the simplest merge algorithm will perform either m comparisons or n comparisons. (m if the first list comes first; n if the second list comes first.) Making O(max?(m,n)).
Looking ahead can let it skip many unnecessary comparisons, but it risks adding wasted comparisons.
Looking ahead once, at the beginning, in the above example with no overlap, would "reduce" the best-case comparisons from max?(m,n) to min(m,n) + log2(m) - 1, or O(min(m,n).)
Looking ahead while merging could avoid many comparisons IF the result isn't tightly interleaved (it receives some long "runs" from either input list). Looking ahead is guesswork, so the better guessing algorithm will be heuristic and a little adaptive. When merging random data, looking ahead by 1 costs a wasted comparison about as often as it saves a comparison. But with non-random data, the net savings can be larger. If long runs exist, adaptively looking ahead by a larger distances could save a lot of comparisons. You could do way better than O(m+n), depending on your skill at making the guessing algorithm and its match to the distributions of the actual nonrandom data. You'll need an algorithm for the forward guess (twice as far ahead as last time?) and one for the fallback guesses after a wrong guess (half as far ahead as the last guess?).
Another way to describe this approach is: After picking a side, see how many more in a row you can take from that side without checking every element within the run.

Q: ggplot2 and gridExtra: completely remove strip in facet_grid - not just invisible A:

With current ggplot2, you can also place the strip inside the figure and make it blank to achieve the desired effect:

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) + geom_point()
p2 <- p2 + facet_grid(cyl ~ .) +
  theme(
    strip.text.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text.y = element_blank(),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.placement = "inside"
  )
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=1)

Q: Working with missing value code without replacing value to NA A: 
You can handle -9999 as a missing value without changing the original columns. The easiest way is to create a temporary copy of the columns, replace -9999 with NA in that copy, and then calculate the row averages.

Base R
df <- data.frame(
  v1 = c(-9999, 76, 68),
  v2 = c(81, 72, 65),
  v3 = c(73, 70, -9999)
)

vars <- c("v1", "v2", "v3")

df$average <- rowMeans(
  replace(df[vars], df[vars] == -9999, NA),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

df

The result will be:

     v1 v2    v3  average
1 -9999 81    73 77.00000
2    76 72    70 72.66667
3    68 65 -9999 66.50000

The nice thing about this approach is that replace() works on a temporary copy. So the -9999 values in your original v1, v2, and v3 columns are not changed.

Then rowMeans() calculates the average and na.rm = TRUE tells R to ignore the NA values.

Using dplyr

If you prefer working with pipes, you can do the same thing like this:

library(dplyr)

df %>%
  mutate(
    average = rowMeans(
      across(v1:v3, ~ na_if(.x, -9999)),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

Here, na_if() treats -9999 as NA only for the calculation. The original columns remain unchanged.
